title: Time
note: Several time words keep a Latin root in view: diurnal (dies, day), vernal (ver, spring), quotidian (quotidie, every day), antediluvian (before the flood). Incipient and inchoate both describe beginnings: incipient things are just starting to appear, while inchoate things are still unformed. Imminent means about to happen; do not confuse it with eminent, distinguished.

items.a: quickly fading or vanishing
items.ex: The evanescent glow of the sunset lasted barely a minute.

items.a: lasting only a short time; passing
items.ex: The pain was transient, gone by morning.

items.a: extending back beyond memory or record
items.ex: Shepherds have used these trails since time immemorial.

items.a: extremely old-fashioned or outdated
items.ex: The office ran on an antediluvian computer with a green screen.

items.a: very old or no longer in ordinary use
items.ex: "Thou" sounds archaic to most English speakers today.

items.a: something placed in the wrong historical period
items.ex: A wristwatch on a Roman soldier is an anachronism.

items.a: existing from the very beginning of time
items.ex: Scientists study meteorites for clues to the primordial solar system.

items.a: just beginning to appear or develop
items.ex: She caught the incipient leak before it ruined the ceiling.

items.a: only partly formed; not yet developed
items.ex: His plan was still inchoate, a few arrows on a napkin.

items.a: a sign or forerunner of what is to come
d: a relic of the distant past
items.ex: The first robin is a harbinger of spring.

items.a: to be a warning or sign of a future event
d: to happen at the same time
items.ex: The tremors may presage a larger eruption.

items.a: having knowledge of events before they happen
items.ex: Her prescient 2005 essay predicted the housing crash.

items.a: promising success; favorable
items.ex: Rain on the wedding day is considered auspicious in some cultures.

items.a: slow to act; causing delay
items.ex: The court fined the dilatory lawyer for missing three deadlines.

items.a: lasting longer than expected or usual
items.ex: The protracted negotiations dragged into a second year.

items.a: seemingly endless, and tiresome
items.ex: The flight's delay was announced in interminable fifteen-minute installments.

items.a: occurring at irregular intervals; scattered
items.ex: Sporadic gunfire continued after the ceasefire.

items.a: continuing without pause
items.ex: The incessant barking next door kept the street awake.

items.a: occurring daily, or active in the daytime
items.ex: Squirrels are diurnal; raccoons prefer the night.

items.a: relating to twilight, or active at twilight
items.ex: Deer are crepuscular, most active at dawn and dusk.

items.a: relating to or occurring in spring
items.ex: The vernal equinox falls around March 20.

items.a: ordinary; occurring every day
items.ex: The novel finds beauty in quotidian chores like folding laundry.

items.a: idyllically calm and happy, especially of a past time
items.ex: He spoke of the halcyon summers at the lake before the highway came.

items.a: a pause or break in continuity
items.ex: The band returned after a ten-year hiatus.

items.a: a temporary ban or suspension of an activity
d: a sign of things to come
items.ex: The city declared a moratorium on new parking lots.

items.a: former; in the past
items.ex: The erstwhile rivals now run a bakery together.

items.a: occurring after a person's death
items.ex: Emily Dickinson's fame was almost entirely posthumous.

items.a: existing or occurring in the same period
items.ex: Contemporaneous newspaper accounts contradict the memoir.

items.a: about to happen
items.ex: Forecasters warned that landfall was imminent.

items.a: to stall or delay in order to gain time
d: to happen at the same time
items.ex: The mayor temporized, promising a study instead of a decision.
